new_slides.title: Air pushed ahead of a predator reaches the cerci first
body: A body moving through air displaces the air in front of it, so a current spreads ahead of an approaching predator before any contact. Filiform hairs are long and light, and the drag of even a faint current deflects them, which is why restrained cockroaches responded to air moving at only a few millimeters per second.

The arrival of a puff produces a synchronous burst of afferent activity, and the phasic ascending interneurons with the largest axons respond to the acceleration component of the wind, the part that initiates the escape turn. A gust that builds suddenly is therefore a stronger trigger than a steady breeze of similar speed.

An approaching toad generates such an accelerating flow. Sensitivity to the onset of air movement plausibly allows the cockroach to respond early in an attack while remaining less driven by the slow, steady air movements that surround it.

figure.caption: Camhi et al. (1978), Fig. 3(B). Wind trace near the behavioral response threshold.

new_slides.cite: Camhi et al. (1978); Olsen & Triblehorn (2014); McGorry et al. (2014)
transcript: Slides 2 and 6 establish that airflow from a toad arrives before the tongue; the physical reason is that any moving body pushes a column of air ahead of itself. The cockroach's cerci face backward and outward, so they sample air arriving from behind and to the sides, where an attacker is hardest to see.
The hairs are mechanically suited to faint currents.
A long, light hair offers a large surface to the moving air while having little mass to accelerate, so small drag forces are enough to deflect it.
The threshold of about three thousandths of a meter per second on slide 6 reflects that sensitivity in a restrained animal.
Onset and steady flow are encoded differently.
Olsen and Triblehorn describe an initial positive peak in the afferent recording generated by synchronous activity as the wind arrives at the cerci.

McGorry and colleagues relate the first hundred milliseconds of a puff, which contain its acceleration, to initiation of the escape turn, and the later constant-velocity part to continued running and flight.
Responding to change rather than to a constant level is a common sensory strategy.
A sensor that signals mainly when its input changes reports new events strongly and adapts to background conditions.
For the cockroach, the new event is the gust produced by something moving toward it.
refs: Camhi, J. M., Tom, W., & Volman, S. (1978). The escape behavior of the cockroach Periplaneta americana. II. Detection of natural predators by air displacement. Journal of Comparative Physiology, 128, 203–212. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00656853

Olsen, A. C. K., & Triblehorn, J. D. (2014). Neural responses from the filiform receptor neuron afferents of the wind-sensitive cercal system in three cockroach species. Journal of Insect Physiology, 68, 76–86. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinsphys.2014.07.002

McGorry, C. A., Newman, C. N., & Triblehorn, J. D. (2014). Neural responses from the wind-sensitive interneuron population in four cockroach species. Journal of Insect Physiology, 66, 59–70. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinsphys.2014.05.017

new_slides.title: Each hair moves in one plane, giving it a preferred wind axis
body: A filiform hair sits in a socket that allows it to swing more easily along one axis than along others. Deflection along that axis stretches the dendrite of the receptor neuron at its base, opening mechanically gated ion channels and producing spikes, so each receptor fires best to wind blowing along its hair's plane of movement.

Hairs on a cercus have their planes of movement oriented in different directions, so any one puff activates a characteristic subset. Each cercus also responds more strongly to wind from its own side, the external direction, than from the opposite side, giving the two cerci complementary views of the same current.

The nervous system reads direction from which hairs are active, assuming their normal orientation on the body. Rotating the cerci keeps that reading rule but changes which hairs a given wind activates, so the animal turns as if the wind came from a shifted direction.

figure.caption: Camhi & Tom (1978), Fig. 10. Turning after clockwise cercal rotation.

transcript: Slides 8 to 10 locate the wind detector on the ventral cercal surface and establish that rotating the cerci shifts the turn. The mechanical design of each hair explains both results.
Directional tuning begins in the socket.

A hair that can swing in only one plane converts wind from other directions into a smaller deflection, so its receptor responds most to wind along that plane and progressively less as the wind angle departs from it.
Mechanically gated channels in the receptor's dendrite open when the hair's base is displaced, turning movement into an electrical signal.
Direction is coded by which receptors are active.
Different hairs have different preferred axes and positions, and Jankowska and colleagues report that each hair has a specific location and set of biomechanical features.
Their recordings found larger cercal nerve responses when each cercus was stimulated from its external side than from the internal side.
The rotation experiment exploits this arrangement.
After rotation, a wind from a fixed source deflects hairs whose orientation the nervous system still interprets in their original frame, so the computed direction shifts.
Covering the ventral surface, by contrast, removes the active hairs altogether, which explains why it abolished responses instead of redirecting them.
refs: Camhi, J. M., & Tom, W. (1978). The escape behavior of the cockroach Periplaneta americana. I. Turning response to wind puffs. Journal of Comparative Physiology, 128, 193–201. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00656852

Jankowska, M., Klimek, A., Valsecchi, C., Stankiewicz, M., Wyszkowska, J., & Rogalska, J. (2021). Electromagnetic field and TGF-β enhance the compensatory plasticity after sensory nerve injury in cockroach Periplaneta americana. Scientific Reports, 11, 6582. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-85341-z

new_slides.title: Synchronous input spikes sum more effectively downstream
body: Each spike arriving at a synapse produces a brief postsynaptic potential in the interneuron that decays within milliseconds. Potentials arriving close together add before decaying, a process called **temporal summation**, whereas widely spaced potentials largely decay independently.

Many afferents converging on one interneuron combine in the same way across cells. When they fire in synchrony, their potentials coincide and are more likely to carry the interneuron past threshold than the same number of spikes spread out in time. Olsen and Triblehorn report that afferent number, spikes per afferent and synchrony all shape activation of the following stage.

Synchrony therefore offers a way for a species with fewer hairs to drive its interneurons strongly. In _B. craniifer_, a larger second afferent peak coincided with longer-lasting high interneuron firing, the pattern expected when tightly timed afferent spikes summate onto the giants.

figure.caption: Olsen & Triblehorn (2014), Fig. 4(A–C). Species differences in wind-response timing.

transcript: Slides 11 to 14 describe synchrony as a property of the afferent recording; its importance comes from how the receiving interneuron integrates input. A postsynaptic potential is a transient voltage change that fades as current leaks out of the cell.
Timing determines how inputs combine.
If a second potential arrives before the first has faded, the two add, so the peak voltage is higher than either alone.
If it arrives after the first has decayed, the cell must start again from near rest, so the same two inputs have much less effect on firing.
Convergence makes synchrony matter at the population level.
Many receptor axons from the same cercus end on the same wind-sensitive interneuron in the terminal ganglion.
When a sudden gust deflects many hairs at once, their spikes arrive together and summate strongly, which favors a rapid interneuron response.
The species comparison makes the point concrete.
The species with about sixty hairs per cercus produced afferent and interneuron responses as large as, or larger than, the species with about two hundred.
Olsen and Triblehorn proposed greater synchrony as one reason; individual-cell recordings would be needed to test it.
refs: Olsen, A. C. K., & Triblehorn, J. D. (2014). Neural responses from the filiform receptor neuron afferents of the wind-sensitive cercal system in three cockroach species. Journal of Insect Physiology, 68, 76–86. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinsphys.2014.07.002

McGorry, C. A., Newman, C. N., & Triblehorn, J. D. (2014). Neural responses from the wind-sensitive interneuron population in four cockroach species. Journal of Insect Physiology, 66, 59–70. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinsphys.2014.05.017

new_slides.title: Detecting wind and measuring its speed are different jobs
body: A sensory pathway can act as an on/off switch, signaling only that a stimulus crossed a threshold, or as a dimmer, grading its output over many intensities. The **dynamic range**, the span of stimulus strengths over which the response keeps changing, indicates which job a pathway suits.

McGorry and colleagues found that the two species with strong terrestrial escape had the narrowest interneuron dynamic range during wind onset, about half that of the other two. For starting an escape, knowing that a sudden gust occurred may matter more than knowing its exact speed.

Steady airflow is used differently. In flying cockroaches the cercal system monitors wind during flight, where graded velocity information can guide steering, so one pathway can support a switch-like trigger at onset and graded encoding later.

figure.caption: Olsen & Triblehorn (2014), Fig. 5(A–D). Early and later afferent stimulus–response curves.

transcript: Slides 12 and 14 present stimulus–response curves for the first hundred and the following hundred and fifty milliseconds; the authors' interpretation of those curves distinguishes detecting an event from measuring its size.
A switch and a dimmer have different useful properties.
A pathway that saturates quickly is reliable at signaling that something happened but carries little information about how strong it was.
A pathway that keeps changing over a wide range carries magnitude information but may respond less decisively near threshold.
The comparison across species supports the switch interpretation for escape.
The two strong escapers had dynamic ranges almost half those of the other species during onset.
McGorry and colleagues suggest that, for initiating escape, the cercal system may simply monitor whether wind exceeds a threshold velocity.
Graded information is still available later in the stimulus.
The constant-velocity part of a puff is the part the cercal system uses to maintain and adjust flight in flying species, and it may also guide the running phase.
The same anatomical pathway therefore serves two functions that differ in what they need to encode.
refs: Olsen, A. C. K., & Triblehorn, J. D. (2014). Neural responses from the filiform receptor neuron afferents of the wind-sensitive cercal system in three cockroach species. Journal of Insect Physiology, 68, 76–86. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinsphys.2014.07.002

McGorry, C. A., Newman, C. N., & Triblehorn, J. D. (2014). Neural responses from the wind-sensitive interneuron population in four cockroach species. Journal of Insect Physiology, 66, 59–70. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinsphys.2014.05.017

new_slides.title: Wide axons carry the warning to the thorax faster
body: A spike travels by spreading current ahead of itself inside the axon until neighboring membrane reaches threshold. Internal resistance to that current falls as the axon widens, so current spreads farther and faster, and conduction speed rises with diameter in unmyelinated axons such as insect giant interneurons.

Giant interneurons gain speed this way along the long path from the terminal ganglion to the thoracic motor circuits. Their size also makes them identifiable: extracellular spike amplitude grows with axon diameter, which is how comparative recordings link the largest units to the phasic interneurons that initiate escape.

The giants are one link in a short chain: one synapse from receptor to giant, a fast ascending axon, then premotor and motor neurons, which brings the first leg movement within tens of milliseconds of the air current's arrival.

figure.caption: Booth et al. (2009), Fig. 1(A,B). Second-instar animal and its cercal sensory circuit.

new_slides.cite: Booth et al. (2009); McGorry et al. (2014)
transcript: Slide 16 introduces the giant axon as the ascending path; the reason a large axon matters is the physics of conduction.
Wider axons conduct faster.
The current that depolarizes the membrane ahead of a spike flows along the inside of the axon, and a wider core offers it less resistance.
Insects have no myelin, so axon diameter is the main way to increase conduction speed, which is why giant axons recur in fast escape systems.
Size also leaves a signature in recordings.
McGorry and colleagues report that extracellular spike amplitude correlates with axon diameter, so the largest units in a connective recording are the largest axons.
Those large, phasic units responded strongly to the onset of wind, matching the role of the giants in starting escape.
The whole chain is built for speed.
The direct sensory-to-giant synapse on slide 15 avoids extra synaptic delays at the first stage.
The behavioral latency of about fifty-eight milliseconds on slide 6 includes receptor activation, conduction, synapses in the thorax and muscle activation; shortening any link shortens the whole.
refs: Booth, D., Marie, B., Domenici, P., Blagburn, J. M., & Bacon, J. P. (2009). Transcriptional control of behavior: engrailed knock-out changes cockroach escape trajectories. Journal of Neuroscience, 29(22), 7181–7190. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1374-09.2009

McGorry, C. A., Newman, C. N., & Triblehorn, J. D. (2014). Neural responses from the wind-sensitive interneuron population in four cockroach species. Journal of Insect Physiology, 66, 59–70. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinsphys.2014.05.017

new_slides.title: A single GI's firing is ambiguous about wind direction
body: A broadly tuned neuron responds similarly to wind from two directions on either side of its preferred direction. Its firing also rises with wind strength, so a weak puff on its preferred axis and a stronger puff off it can give the same spike count.

Comparing several neurons removes that ambiguity. Each source angle produces a distinct ratio of activity across GI1, GI2 and GI3 on the two sides, and a ratio stays the same when overall wind strength changes, since a stronger puff raises activity in all the cells together.

This is the advantage of a **population code** over a **labeled line**, in which one dedicated neuron signals one direction. Six broadly tuned cells represent a continuous range of angles, and losing one cell shifts the estimate instead of abolishing it.

figure.caption: Levi & Camhi (2000b), Fig. 1(A). Adult GI directional profiles used as model inputs.

transcript: Slides 17 and 18 establish that the GIs' directional profiles overlap broadly; the reason the nervous system benefits from that overlap is that no single broadly tuned cell can specify direction by itself.
A single cell confounds direction with strength.
A given spike count could mean wind slightly to one side of the preferred direction or slightly to the other side.
It could also mean a weak puff on the preferred axis or a strong puff off it, since firing rises with wind velocity.
Ratios across cells solve both problems.
Two cells with different preferred directions respond in a ratio that changes systematically with wind angle.
A stronger puff scales both responses together, so the ratio, and with it the estimated direction, is preserved.
The population arrangement explains the later intervention results.
Removing GI2's contribution on slide 30 changed the turn instead of abolishing it, which is what a population estimate predicts when one member is lost.
A labeled-line code would instead predict loss of responses specifically for the lost cell's direction.
refs: Levi, R., & Camhi, J. M. (2000b). Population vector coding by the giant interneurons of the cockroach. Journal of Neuroscience, 20(10), 3822–3829. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.20-10-03822.2000

new_slides.title: Winner-take-all requires strong mutual inhibition
body: A winner-take-all circuit is built from **mutual inhibition**: each pathway suppresses the others, so the most active one silences its rivals and alone drives the output, and small changes near the balance point flip the output abruptly.

In a summing circuit each input adds its weighted contribution downstream, so the output varies smoothly with the balance of inputs. Levi and Camhi's graded results with spikes added to GI3 and to opposite-side GIs fit this arrangement, in which both sides contribute to every turn.

Summation allows turn size to match the wind angle, including intermediate angles. With every giant interneuron contributing on every trial, noise in any one cell shifts the turn slightly instead of reversing it, and the population as a whole sets the escape heading.

figure.caption: Levi & Camhi (2000a), Fig. 8(A,B). Turning changes after adding left-side GI spikes.

transcript: Slides 25 and 26 rule out a strong winner-take-all mechanism from the graded behavioral results; the circuit difference between the two alternatives explains why gradedness is the decisive observation.
Mutual inhibition produces abrupt switches.
When two pathways inhibit each other strongly, a small advantage for one reduces the other's activity, which further increases the first one's advantage.
This self-reinforcing competition drives the circuit to one extreme or the other, so intermediate outputs are rare.
Summation produces graded outputs.
If downstream neurons simply add the weighted inputs from each GI, increasing one input moves the output gradually.
The progressive change in left-turning tendency as added spike frequency increased on slides 25 and 26 matches this prediction.
Gradedness has a behavioral benefit.
A turn whose size follows the wind angle sends the animal more directly away from the threat than a choice among a few fixed turns would.
Levi and Camhi describe direction as determined by a collaborative calculation among the giant interneurons as a group.
refs: Levi, R., & Camhi, J. M. (2000a). Wind direction coding in the cockroach escape response: winner does not take all. Journal of Neuroscience, 20(10), 3814–3821. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.20-10-03814.2000

new_slides.title: Adding, removing and replacing activity test different claims
body: Two questions run through the cockroach experiments. **Necessity** asks whether a response fails without a component; **sufficiency** asks whether supplying the component can produce or change the response. Each calls for a different manipulation, and neither answers the other.

Waxing the ventral cercal hairs and photoablating GI2 removed components and tested necessity. Adding spikes to GI3 or to opposite-side GIs tested whether a cell's activity is sufficient to change turning. Replacing GI2 spikes after ablation combined both: a loss followed by restoration of the same signal.

Rescue is the strongest of these designs. If a lesion's effect came from incidental damage, supplying the missing spikes should not reverse it, so partial reversal ties the behavioral change to GI2's activity rather than to the injury that removed it.

figure.caption: Levi & Camhi (2000b), Fig. 7(A,B). Natural GI2 firing and partial behavioral rescue.

transcript: The deck contains every major type of causal intervention, from coating the cerci to adding, removing and replacing identified spikes. Sorting them by the question each answers clarifies what has and has not been established.
Removal experiments test necessity.
Covering the ventral cercal hairs on slide 9 abolished responses, so the hair field is necessary for the wind-evoked turn.
Photoablation on slide 29 removed GI2's wind-driven activity and changed the turn, so GI2 contributes to the normal turning measure.
Addition experiments test sufficiency to change behavior.
Adding spikes to right GI3 on slide 23 and to left GIs on slide 26 altered turning while the wind stayed the same.
These results establish that a single cell's activity can shift the output; they do not establish that the cell could produce escape on its own.
Rescue closes the main loophole of lesions.
A lesion can act through damage, inflammation or loss of a cell's other functions.
Returning only the spikes and seeing the behavior move back toward normal on slide 31 attributes the lesion's effect to the missing activity.
refs: Camhi, J. M., & Tom, W. (1978). The escape behavior of the cockroach Periplaneta americana. I. Turning response to wind puffs. Journal of Comparative Physiology, 128, 193–201. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00656852

Levi, R., & Camhi, J. M. (2000a). Wind direction coding in the cockroach escape response: winner does not take all. Journal of Neuroscience, 20(10), 3814–3821. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.20-10-03814.2000
Levi, R., & Camhi, J. M. (2000b). Population vector coding by the giant interneurons of the cockroach. Journal of Neuroscience, 20(10), 3822–3829. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.20-10-03822.2000

new_slides.title: Keeping a sensor does not mean using it for escape
body: _G. portentosa_ lacks a wind-evoked terrestrial escape and cannot fly, yet it retains ascending wind-sensitive interneurons. A trait can persist from an ancestor even when the behavior it once served has weakened, so the presence of a pathway is evidence about history, not proof of its present use.

The pathway may also serve other behaviors. In flying species the cercal system monitors steady airflow during flight, and McGorry and colleagues suggest that differences in encoding point to other roles for cercal wind information, which remain untested.

_B. craniifer_ shows the opposite mismatch: strong neural responses with weak escape. Escape requires sensory input to engage thoracic motor circuits, so its weak escape points to a change downstream of the interneurons, in premotor coupling or in the decision to run, placing the evolutionary difference at the link between sensing and acting rather than in sensing itself.

figure.caption: McGorry et al. (2014), Fig. 4. Ascending wind responses in four cockroach species.

transcript: Slides 33 and 34 establish that wind sensitivity and escape behavior do not track each other across species. Separating the existence of a pathway from its current use explains both mismatches.
A retained pathway can reflect shared ancestry.
All four species belong to a group in which the cercal system is widespread, so a species that no longer escapes from wind may still carry the inherited sensory machinery.
Whether that machinery now serves another purpose in such species is an open question.
Sensory strength does not guarantee motor use.
_B. craniifer_ had afferent and interneuron responses as strong as the strong escapers, yet weak escape behavior.
McGorry and colleagues suggest reexamining its behavior and investigating the neural mechanisms between interneurons and motor circuits.
The comparison exemplifies a general method.
Species that differ in behavior while sharing a circuit allow researchers to ask which stage of the circuit accounts for the behavioral difference.
Here the afferent and interneuron stages were measured; the premotor and motor stages were not.
refs: Olsen, A. C. K., & Triblehorn, J. D. (2014). Neural responses from the filiform receptor neuron afferents of the wind-sensitive cercal system in three cockroach species. Journal of Insect Physiology, 68, 76–86. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinsphys.2014.07.002

McGorry, C. A., Newman, C. N., & Triblehorn, J. D. (2014). Neural responses from the wind-sensitive interneuron population in four cockroach species. Journal of Insect Physiology, 66, 59–70. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jinsphys.2014.05.017

new_slides.title: Several preferred trajectories keep escape unpredictable
body: A predator that learns where prey will run can intercept it. Booth and colleagues describe cockroaches as keeping each escape unpredictable by choosing among a set of preferred trajectories at fixed angles from the threat, with wind direction shifting the odds among them rather than fixing one path.

This combines two requirements. Each preferred trajectory leads away from the threat, so escape remains effective, while the choice among them varies between attempts, so a predator cannot anticipate the exact path.

The probabilities of choosing each trajectory depend on perceived wind direction. Any change in how direction is encoded should therefore appear as a change in which trajectories are chosen, which makes trajectory distributions a sensitive readout of the sensory circuit.

figure.caption: Booth et al. (2009), Fig. 5(C–H). Juvenile trajectories by wind direction and En treatment.

transcript: Slides 35 and 36 describe juvenile cockroaches using several preferred escape trajectories, with wind direction changing how often each is used. The functional reason for this arrangement is that predictable prey are easier to catch.
Variability is itself a defense.
A toad or other predator that has experienced many escapes could, in principle, learn to strike where prey usually run.
Distributing escapes among several fixed trajectories prevents any single path from being reliably predicted.
The trajectories are not random.
Each trajectory lies at a fixed angle from the stimulus, so all of them move the animal away from the threat.
Wind direction changes the probability of each trajectory, which keeps escape adaptive while preserving unpredictability.
This organization makes the En experiments interpretable.
A change in perceived direction should shift the probabilities toward the trajectories appropriate to the perceived direction.
That is exactly the type of change measured after Engrailed knock-down on slide 40.
refs: Booth, D., Marie, B., Domenici, P., Blagburn, J. M., & Bacon, J. P. (2009). Transcriptional control of behavior: engrailed knock-out changes cockroach escape trajectories. Journal of Neuroscience, 29(22), 7181–7190. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1374-09.2009

new_slides.title: Engrailed tells a sensory neuron which giants to contact
body: Engrailed is expressed only in sensory neurons born on the medial side of the cercus, so it can mark position. Earlier work summarized by Booth and colleagues found that removing Engrailed changed the axon branching and synaptic outputs of an identified Engrailed-positive neuron until it resembled an Engrailed-negative neighbor.

A transcription factor can do this by controlling genes that steer a growing axon and select its synaptic partners, linking a neuron's position on the cercus, and so its directional tuning, to the giants that receive its signal.

Miswiring changes what the giants report. If a medial neuron connects like a lateral one, its wind information reaches the wrong interneurons, and the directional pattern across the giants no longer matches the wind.

figure.caption: Booth et al. (2009), Fig. 2(A,B). Second-instar En staining before and after RNAi.

transcript: Slides 37 and 38 establish that Engrailed is expressed in medial sensory neurons and that RNA interference reduces it. The link to behavior runs through wiring, which Booth and colleagues summarize from their own earlier identified-neuron work.
Position determines identity, and identity determines connections.
Neurons born at different positions on the cercus carry hairs with different locations and directional properties.
A positional transcription factor ensures that a neuron with a particular directional input connects to the interneurons that should receive that information.
The earlier experiment tested this directly.
After Engrailed was removed, an identified Engrailed-positive neuron changed its axon projections and synaptic outputs until it resembled an Engrailed-negative neighbor.
The neighbor itself was unaffected, which ties the change to the loss of Engrailed in the expressing cell.
The consequence is a sensory error, not a motor one.
Interneurons that receive the wrong mix of directional inputs report a distorted wind direction, even though the motor circuits downstream are intact.
Booth and colleagues describe this as the first evidence that knocking down a transcription factor controlling synaptic connectivity can alter perception of a directional stimulus.
refs: Booth, D., Marie, B., Domenici, P., Blagburn, J. M., & Bacon, J. P. (2009). Transcriptional control of behavior: engrailed knock-out changes cockroach escape trajectories. Journal of Neuroscience, 29(22), 7181–7190. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1374-09.2009

new_slides.title: Knock-down animals act as if rear wind came from the front
body: The trajectories chosen after Engrailed knock-down were those normally used for anterior wind. Booth and colleagues interpret this as altered perception: the miswired circuit reports rear wind as coming from farther forward, and the animal responds appropriately to the direction its giants signal.

This interpretation separates two possible failures. A motor defect would disturb trajectory choice for all wind directions; a sensory misreport predicts errors confined to the directions served by the miswired neurons, which matches the selective effect on posterior wind.

The proposed chain runs from gene to wiring to perception: reduced Engrailed changes which giants the medial sensory neurons contact, their receptive fields shift, and the animal picks trajectories for the direction its giants report.

figure.caption: Booth et al. (2009), Fig. 6(A–F). Third-instar trajectories after En reduction.

transcript: Slide 40 reports that knock-down animals made more small-angle escapes and more turns toward the source for rearward wind. Reading these as perceptual errors explains why they take the specific form they do.
The animals behaved correctly for the wrong direction.
Choosing trajectories suited to anterior wind when wind comes from behind is what an intact motor system would do if it received a forward-shifted direction signal.
The abstract of the study describes the effect as altering the choice of trajectories to one more appropriate for anterior wind.
Selectivity argues against a general impairment.
Responses to anterior wind were comparatively preserved, so the animals could still detect wind, run and choose among trajectories.
An error limited to one range of wind directions points to the part of the sensory map served by the affected neurons.
The inference has a measured and a predicted part.
Reduced Engrailed staining and the altered trajectories were measured directly in the same animals.
Changes in giant receptive fields were predicted from connectivity, so recordings from juvenile GIs after knock-down are the direct test still needed.
refs: Booth, D., Marie, B., Domenici, P., Blagburn, J. M., & Bacon, J. P. (2009). Transcriptional control of behavior: engrailed knock-out changes cockroach escape trajectories. Journal of Neuroscience, 29(22), 7181–7190. https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1374-09.2009

new_slides.title: Deprived giants may strengthen the surviving cercal input
body: Each giant interneuron normally receives input from both cerci, and loss of one cercus leaves its share of synapses silent as the cut sensory axons degenerate. Jankowska and colleagues propose that the deprived interneurons release **retrograde messengers**, signals sent from postsynaptic to presynaptic cells, that alter the surviving sensory neurons.

When several axons compete for trophic factors supplied by a target cell, inactive endings lose out and active ones are strengthened. Removing right-cercus input could tip that competition toward left-cercus synapses, and changes in the sensory neurons' own excitability could add to the effect.

Left-cercus nerve responses to right-side wind grew, but connective responses to the same stimulus did not, which the authors take as evidence that the sensitized sensory neurons formed no new connections onto the giants.

figure.caption: Jankowska et al. (2021), Fig. 2(a,b). Left-cercal nerve responses over three weeks after injury.

transcript: Slides 42 to 44 report increased responsiveness in the surviving pathway after cercus removal; the discussion of the paper proposes how such compensation could arise.
The giants are the deprived partners.
Sensory cells from each cercus connect to giant interneurons through ipsilateral and contralateral projections, so losing one cercus removes part of the input to giants on both sides.
The authors suggest that this reduced stimulation triggers a retrograde reaction in the giants.
Two kinds of plasticity are proposed.
Synaptic plasticity would strengthen the connections from the surviving cercus, for example through competition for trophic factors.
Non-synaptic plasticity would change the intrinsic properties of the surviving sensory neurons, making them more responsive to stimulation from the lost side.
Recording at two levels separates these possibilities.
A change in the cercal nerve without a matching change in the connective points to altered sensory neurons rather than new synapses.
The connective did increase for left-side stimulation after two weeks, which the authors attribute to sensory changes, stronger synapses, or both.
refs: Jankowska, M., Klimek, A., Valsecchi, C., Stankiewicz, M., Wyszkowska, J., & Rogalska, J. (2021). Electromagnetic field and TGF-β enhance the compensatory plasticity after sensory nerve injury in cockroach Periplaneta americana. Scientific Reports, 11, 6582. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-85341-z

new_slides.title: Left-right decisions rely on comparing the two cerci
body: Each cercus responds more strongly to wind from its own side, so comparing activity between the two indicates whether a puff comes from the left or the right. Giant interneurons on each side receive input from both cerci, and the turn depends on activity across both sides.

Losing one cercus removes half of that comparison. Wind from either side now reaches only one sensory organ, and its stronger response to its own side cannot by itself distinguish a weak puff from that side from a strong puff from the other.

Rotating the cerci shifted perceived direction, and spikes added to opposite-side giants could reverse turns, both evidence that direction is computed from the balance of bilateral input. Restoring accurate escape after injury would therefore require the surviving input to recreate that balance, not just to grow larger.

figure.caption: Jankowska et al. (2021), Fig. 3(a–d). Peripheral and central responses with field exposure.

new_slides.cite: Camhi & Tom (1978); Levi & Camhi (2000a); Jankowska et al. (2021)
transcript: Slides 42 to 45 test recovery after losing one cercus with nerve recordings and an arena assay. The importance of a bilateral comparison explains why neither measure establishes recovery of directional escape.
Two cerci provide a built-in comparison.
Jankowska and colleagues found larger cercal nerve responses when each cercus was stimulated from its external side.
A difference between left and right responses therefore signals the side of the stimulus, independent of how strong the stimulus is.
One cercus confounds side with strength.
With only the left cercus, a strong puff from the right and a weak puff from the left could produce similar activity.
Greater sensitivity to right-side wind, as found after three weeks, increases the signal but does not by itself restore a left-right comparison.
The deck's other experiments point to the same balance.
Cercal rotation on slide 10 shifted the computed direction, and added left-GI spikes on slide 26 could change the sign of the turning measure.
Both results indicate that direction emerges from comparing inputs across the two sides, which is what injury disrupts.
